headline: Revolut confirms customer data breach via fake government requests
summary: British fintech Revolut disclosed sensitive customer data to an unauthorized third party after falling for fraudulent requests from a legitimate government email domain. Exposed data includes identity, contact details, and copies of ID documents.
details: British fintech Revolut has confirmed a data breach, disclosing sensitive customer information to an unauthorized third party. This occurred after the company received fraudulent requests sent from a legitimate government agency email domain.

The exposed data included customers’ identity and contact details, such as birth date, postal and email addresses, and phone numbers. Copies of identity documents like passports and driver’s licenses were also compromised.

Revolut stated that verification selfies, account statements, and transaction histories may also have been included. A "limited" number of customers were impacted, and the company has directly notified those affected.

The incident involved a "sophisticated external impersonation scam" where the third party exploited a genuine government email domain. Revolut blocked the email address and alerted the relevant government agency, law enforcement, and regulators.

Despite the data disclosure, Revolut maintains that its internal systems and customer funds remain unaffected. The company did not disclose the exact number of impacted individuals or the specific government agency involved.

Revolut, a London-based fintech, serves over 80 million customers globally and operates as a bank in more than 30 countries. The incident comes as the company reportedly considers a potential public listing.
Crypto security researcher ZachXBT brought attention to Revolut’s notification email, suggesting the breach might have targeted high net worth users.

headline: AI finds 6,202 critical software vulnerabilities, but only 97 patched in two months
summary: Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview identified thousands of high-severity flaws in open-source software, revealing a critical bottleneck in human-speed remediation.
details: In April 2026, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, granting technology leaders and critical infrastructure providers early access to Claude Mythos Preview. This specialized security model was built for vulnerability discovery and defensive analysis.

The findings were stark: out of an estimated 6,202 high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities identified across foundational open-source software, only 97 had been confirmed remediated within two months.

Anthropic noted that "even at our relatively slow pace of disclosures, Mythos Preview is adding to an already-overloaded security ecosystem." This statement exposes that finding defects was never the primary limitation; remediation velocity is.

The core problem is what happens to software reliability when vulnerability discovery operates at machine speed, but remediation operates at human organizational speed. AI has blown this gap wide open.

Modern enterprise software rarely has a clean, greenfield architecture, often spanning decades of accumulated patterns. Enterprise patch delivery typically navigates a heavily gated sequence, including architecture review, compliance gates, and multiple approvals.

This process protects operational stability but was designed for an era when discovery was slow. Gartner's Q2 2026 Emerging Risk Report named AI-driven vulnerability discovery the #1 emerging enterprise risk, warning of its potential to outpace organizational defenses.

Consider Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228): remediation dragged on for months not because patching was hard, but because discovering every transitive instance across complex build graphs was an architectural nightmare. AI can now map those paths instantly; organizational patch delivery remains human-bound.

This issue extends beyond backend systems to modern mobile apps, which are stateful edge nodes in distributed systems. A modern iOS app coordinates native Swift layers, feature flags, remote configs, local caches, and multiple authentication states.

Historically, mobile teams treated edge-case defects like memory leaks or race conditions as simple correctness bugs rather than security boundaries. AI reasoning models are now erasing that distinction, identifying how isolated correctness bugs compound into exploitable attack chains.

For example, an app handling Universal Links might have business logic assuming prior authentication before routing executes. AI analysis easily surfaces such architectural flaws in sequencing assumptions across boundaries, which linters or unit tests might miss.

Compounding the problem, a 2025 study across USF, the Vector Institute, and UMass showed that after five iterative rounds of AI refinement, critical vulnerabilities in AI-generated code rose 37.6%. This code often looks idiomatic and compiles, yet quietly introduces structural debt.

The primary responsibility of senior engineers is shifting from "Did we write code correctly?" to "Did we design deterministic system boundaries and automated verification gates?" When discovery outpaces patching, architecture itself becomes the primary security boundary.

Monoliths delay patch releases; decoupling components reduces blast radius and isolates dependency updates. Applying the Strangler Fig Pattern allows teams to extract legacy modules behind clean interface boundaries, translating to isolated Swift Packages or Kotlin Multiplatform modules on mobile.
